AlreadyInitialized.message: Session already initialized on this connection.

Forbidden.message: The authenticated principal does not hold the required grant.

InvalidValue.message: Value does not satisfy the node's schema.

NodeHeld.message: Another session holds this node. Only one may jog an axis at a time; two pendants alternating setpoints on one joint produce motion neither asked for.

NotCallable.message: Node is not a method, or this controller has no command bound to it.

NotInitialized.message: Session not initialized; call initialize first.

NotObservable.message: Node is not observable and cannot be subscribed to.

TooManySubscriptions.message: Subscription limit reached for this connection.

WriteRejected.message: The controller refused the write in its current state.

data.mode: the mode the controller is actually in

WrongMode.message: The controller is not in a mode that permits this command. Jogging is manual-mode only. The mode is not writable over this protocol — on a machine it is a keyswitch, and a client that could turn it would not have been interlocked so much as asked politely.

CallAcceptance.description: The command was accepted for execution. It does not say the machine has finished, or started — watch the axis's state for that.

async.description: True for every command this build declares. Present so a client does not have to assume it.

ClientCapabilities.description: Presence of a key means the client supports the feature. Empty objects are deliberate: they leave room for per-feature options without a breaking change.

NodeDescriptor.description: What a browse returns for one node.

displayUnit.description: Rendering hint for humans, e.g. `degrees`. Never affects the value.

schema.description: JSON Schema for this node's value. Absent for objects.

unit.description: SI unit of the value, e.g. `rad`. Absent when dimensionless.

NodeError.description: A per-node failure inside an otherwise successful batch. Uses the same codes as the top-level errors.

value.description: Type per the node's own schema.

ProtocolVersion.description: Date-stamped protocol revision. Compared for equality, not ordered.

timeBase.description: `ptp` means timestamps from this controller are comparable with those from any other controller on the same time base. `local` means they are not, and a client must not overlay them.

rateHz.description: The rate the controller will actually send at.

Timestamp.description: RFC 3339 with at least millisecond precision, from the controller's clock. Use it for ordering and intervals; only trust it for absolute correlation when the controller reports a PTP-disciplined time base.

value.description: Type per the node's own schema.

info.description:
The JSON-RPC surface of an E-Motion controller.

GENERATED FILE — do not edit. Produced by `mix exmo.openrpc` from the
ExMo Information Model. Change the model, not this document.

## Layering

RFC 6455 WebSocket carries the bytes and provides liveness through its own
ping/pong frames, so there is deliberately no application-level heartbeat
method. JSON-RPC 2.0 provides the envelope, correlation and error codes.
This document describes the interface.

## Nodes are discovered, not declared here

The methods below are the whole method surface. What they operate on is
the controller's Information Model, browsed at runtime. `x-nodes` carries
a snapshot of that model for tooling, but a client should browse rather
than trust it, because a controller can be configured differently from
the build that generated this file.

## Units

Every quantity is SI: metres, radians, seconds, and their derivatives.
There is no unit field on any value. A node's `unit` states what its
number means; a node's `displayUnit` is a rendering hint for humans and
never changes the wire.
info.title: E-Motion Controller Protocol

methods.description:
The first message on every connection. No other method may be called
until this returns and the client has sent `notifications/initialized`.

The client offers the newest revision it speaks. A controller that speaks
it echoes it back; one that does not returns the newest it does speak, and
the client decides whether it can proceed. The controller never guesses.
methods.name: initialize

methods.description: Sent as a JSON-RPC notification once the client accepts the result of `initialize`. The controller treats the session as usable from here.
methods.name: notifications/initialized

methods.description:
Direct children rather than a subtree, because a pendant renders one level
at a time and a whole-model dump is the thing you least want from a
controller with a hundred axes.

Each descriptor carries the node's JSON Schema, so a client learns what a
value is as it discovers the node, and a generated UI can pick a control
without knowing anything about robots.

Omitting `nodeId` browses from the root.
methods.name: nodes/browse
methods.summary: List the direct children of a node.

methods.description:
Batched, because a pendant rendering twenty properties should cost one
round trip rather than twenty.

Results are positional and always the same length as the request. A node
that cannot be read yields an entry carrying an error rather than
collapsing the whole batch — one unreadable node among twenty is a
partial answer, not a failed call.
methods.name: nodes/read
methods.summary: Read one or more node values.

methods.description:
Batched like reads, and like reads the results are positional and
individually fallible.

Deliberately NOT atomic. A batch that half-succeeds reports exactly which
halves, because the alternative — rolling back a write that has already
reached a drive — is not something this layer can honestly offer.
methods.name: nodes/write
methods.summary: Write one or more node values.

methods.description:
Commands are asynchronous and this returns an *acceptance*, not a result.
A CiA 402 enable is three control words through a state machine that may
refuse them; homing takes as long as it takes. A call that blocked until
the drive agreed would describe a machine mid-movement as though it had
stopped.

Watch the axis's `state` for the outcome. It is subscribable, it uses one
vocabulary on every interface, and it is what an operator watches anyway.

Which commands exist depends on how the axis is driven: browse the axis
and call what is there. A PWM servo has no `reset_fault` because it
cannot report a fault.
methods.name: nodes/call

methods.description:
Only nodes whose descriptor reports `observable` may be subscribed to;
anything else is refused rather than silently never delivered.

The requested rate is advisory. The controller returns what it will
actually send at, which may be lower, and clients must read the granted
rate rather than assuming they got what they asked for.

**Updates are conflated, never queued.** A client slower than the stream
receives the newest value and misses the ones between, by design — the
sequence number skips and that is normal. An implementation that buffers
updates turns a momentarily slow client into one that falls permanently
behind, which is worse in every way than dropping a frame.
methods.name: nodes/subscribe
methods.summary: Subscribe to changes on observable nodes.

methods.description: Idempotent. Ending an unknown or already-ended subscription succeeds, because a client tearing down after a reconnect should not have to reason about whether the controller already dropped it.
methods.name: nodes/unsubscribe

methods.description:
Carries the newest value of each changed node in one subscription. `seq`
is monotonic per subscription and **skips** — a gap means values were
conflated away, which is expected and must not be treated as an error or
trigger a resync.

Batched per tick rather than one notification per node, so a six-axis
update is one frame.
methods.name: notifications/nodes/changed
methods.summary: A conflated batch of node values.

servers.description: Controllers advertise themselves over mDNS as `_emotion._tcp`. The client browses for them rather than asking an operator for an address.
servers.name: controller
servers.summary: A controller on the local network

x-nodeErrors.description: Codes that can appear in a NodeError inside a batch result, rather than as a top-level JSON-RPC error.

axes.description: The arm: its joints, and the tool centre point they place. Positions in radians, velocities in rad/s, the tool in metres.
axes.name: Axes

axes.cartesian.description: What the controller is making of the Cartesian motion it has been asked for. Idle unless a Cartesian jog is being held.
axes.cartesian.name: Cartesian

axes.cartesian.joint.description: The axis that is limiting the motion, empty when none is. Populated when `reason` is joint_limit. "The arm stopped" is a support call; "J5 is at its limit" is something an operator can act on without one, and the difference is this node.
axes.cartesian.joint.name: Joint

axes.cartesian.manipulability.description: sqrt(det(J·Jt)) at the current pose, zero at a singularity. Published for a viewport to shade reachability with, and deliberately not what the controller decides on: it describes the pose and not the command, so it collapses identically whether the freedom being lost is one the operator asked for or one they did not.
axes.cartesian.manipulability.name: Manipulability

axes.cartesian.reason.description: Why the motion is limited or refused, empty when it is neither. `rate` — a joint would have to turn faster than it can, which is what approaching a singularity looks like from the rate side. `joint_limit` — a joint is at or approaching the end of its travel; `joint` names it. `tool_speed` — more tool speed was asked for than manual mode allows, which is policy rather than the arm's own limit and never causes a refusal. `singular` — the arm cannot move in the direction asked at all. `unreadable` — a joint could not be read, which is a wiring problem rather than a kinematic one.
axes.cartesian.reason.name: Reason

axes.cartesian.speed_fraction.description: The fraction of the commanded tool speed being delivered, 0 to 1. 1.0 when tracking or idle. Below 1 the joint rates the command asks for exceed what a joint can turn, and the whole vector is scaled — so the direction is exactly as commanded and only the speed gives way.
axes.cartesian.speed_fraction.name: SpeedFraction

axes.cartesian.state.description: idle | tracking | limited | refused | done. `done` is a `move_linear` that has arrived, and is distinct from `idle` on purpose: a finished move and a move that was never asked for should not look the same. `limited` means the motion is on the commanded line and slower than asked; read `speed_fraction` for how much slower and `reason` for why. `refused` means the arm cannot go where it was pointed and has been commanded to zero. Neither is a fault and neither latches: jog somewhere else and the next tick tracks.
axes.cartesian.state.name: State

axes.jog_cartesian.description: Move the tool centre point along or about one axis of the chosen frame, for as long as the client keeps saying so. Held exactly like a joint jog: re-send at around 10 Hz, and the controller commands zero as soon as assertions stop arriving. An assertion refreshes the direction and speed; the controller re-solves from the arm's live joint positions on its own clock, so the path does not depend on how often the client can speak, and the frame is re-resolved with it, so a rotation about a tool axis follows the tool rather than tracing a cone. Solved differentially from where the arm is, so it stays on the configuration it is already in rather than flipping elbow or wrist mid-move. When a joint would have to turn faster than it can, or would run out of travel, or more tool speed is asked for than manual mode allows, the whole joint vector is scaled rather than clamped per joint — the tool stays exactly on the commanded line and the motion slows. Watch `axes.cartesian` for what the controller is making of it: the state, the fraction of commanded speed being delivered, the reason, and the joint responsible when there is one. Approaching a singularity that fraction falls to zero and the jog is refused; use a joint jog, which is the only way out of one.
axes.jog_cartesian.name: JogCartesian

axes.move_linear.description: Move the tool centre point in a straight line to a pose, and stop there. Unlike a jog this is not held: it is sent once and runs to completion, and nothing needs to keep asserting for it to finish — which also means a client that vanishes mid-move does not stop the arm. Translation and rotation are synchronised, so whichever needs longer sets the pace and both arrive together. Solved on the controller's clock from the arm's live pose, under the same rate ceiling, joint limits and tool speed cap as a jog; watch `axes.cartesian` for what it is making of the motion, including `done` when it has arrived. There is no motion queue in this build, so a second move replaces the first rather than following it.
axes.move_linear.name: MoveLinear

axes.tcp.description: Tool centre point, by forward kinematics over the joints above. Position in metres, orientation in radians as fixed-axis roll, pitch and yaw.
axes.tcp.name: TCP

Read-only and deliberately so: on a machine this is a keyswitch, and a client that could turn it in order to be allowed to move the arm would not have been interlocked so much as asked politely. `fault` is reported whenever any axis is faulted, whatever the selector says, because an operator looking at a faulted machine is not helped by being told it is in manual.
